source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models
finding: Codex translated about a quarter of competition problems into Isabelle with no human fix. Most failures were wrong concept alignment, not syntax.
numbers: 150 random MATH problems (50 algebra, 50 number theory, 50 intermediate algebra): 38 perfect translations = 25.3%. Perfect: 13/17/8. Fail-to-align definitions: 10/18/18. Wrong function application: 6/13/16. Missing assumption: 8/9/9. Syntax/type error: 7/2/11. Missing Isabelle definition: 0/12/3.
quote: the majority of the failures are due to the misalignment of informal and formal definitions
limits: Single human judge protocol; 150 items; Codex only; prompt tuned per subject; intermediate algebra used the algebra prompt.
agent_relevance: The main error is semantic mismatch (greatest value to max, n! to fact), so a scaffold should check meaning, not only that the output parses.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models
finding: Scaling helps: BLEU for autoformalization rose steadily from PaLM 8B to 540B, and Codex beat PaLM on BLEU, likely from more formal code in training.
numbers: PaLM 8B to 540B on MATH algebra and number theory subsets; Codex higher than PaLM by BLEU.
limits: BLEU is a weak proxy for correctness (see ProofNet and BEq+ findings); no human grading at this step.
agent_relevance: Capability gain from scale is real but measured with a poor metric; do not trust BLEU-style similarity as a verifier.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models
finding: Autoformalized statements were used to train a prover by expert iteration, giving a new state of the art on miniF2F at that time.
numbers: miniF2F proof success valid/test: base Thor 28.3/29.9; after 1 iteration 36.1/34.0; after 2 iterations 37.3/35.2; PACT 23.9/24.6; FMSCL 33.6/29.6.
limits: Test gain is about 5 points; proof success does not check statement fidelity, so wrong formal statements can still be proved.
agent_relevance: Downstream proof success is an indirect, noisy check that a translation was useful; it does not prove it was faithful.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models
finding: For advanced mathematics, informalization (formal to natural language) worked far better than formalization.
numbers: 38 Isabelle statements informalized by Codex: 36 coherent, 29 (76%) more or less correct, versus 25% perfect for formalization.
limits: Tiny set chosen by an Isabelle expert; relaxed standard because a human reader fills in context.
agent_relevance: Back-translation is easier than forward translation, so it makes a cheap round-trip consistency check (formalize, informalize, compare).

source: Azerbayev et al. (2023) ProofNet: Autoformalizing and Formally Proving Undergraduate-Level Mathematics
finding: Undergraduate statements are much harder than competition ones. Best few-shot Codex with retrieved prompts got 13.4% correct.
numbers: 371 theorem pairs in Lean 3. Codex few-shot: typecheck 4.3%, BLEU 4.7, accuracy 0. Prompt-retrieval Codex: typecheck 23.7%, BLEU 25.1, accuracy 13.4%. Distilled back-translation Codex: typecheck 45.2%, accuracy 16.1%. proofGPT-1.3B back-translation: 19.4% typecheck, 3.2% accuracy.
limits: Table layout read from a text extraction, so row labels are partly inferred; accuracy is manual grading; the Lean 4 ports later found to need fixes (see Poiroux).
agent_relevance: Accuracy under 20% on real textbook statements means an agent must not assume a formalization is right.

source: Azerbayev et al. (2023) ProofNet: Autoformalizing and Formally Proving Undergraduate-Level Mathematics
finding: Typechecking is necessary but far from enough. A model can typecheck 45.2% of outputs while only 16.1% are right.
numbers: Codex distilled back-translation: 45.2% typecheck vs 16.1% accuracy; proofGPT 19.4% vs 3.2%. Informalization: 62.3% accuracy with Codex retrieval, 100% compile.
limits: Only the Codex row has strong accuracy.
agent_relevance: A formal checker accepts many wrong statements; semantic validation needs a separate step.

source: Azerbayev et al. (2023) ProofNet: Autoformalizing and Formally Proving Undergraduate-Level Mathematics
finding: Retrieval of similar examples and back-translated training data both lifted accuracy; models given only fixed few-shot examples scored zero.
numbers: Few-shot Codex accuracy 0 vs retrieval 13.4%; proofGPT few-shot 0 accuracy.
limits: Single benchmark, Lean 3, models from 2022-23.
agent_relevance: Dynamic example retrieval from the target library is a high-leverage moderator.

source: Poiroux et al. (2025) Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization
finding: Type-check rate correlates only modestly with human accuracy, while a symbolic equivalence metric (BEq+) correlates strongly.
numbers: Benchmark-level, 65 data points on ProofNet#: type-check Pearson 0.655 / Kendall 0.560; BEqL 0.966 / 0.846; BEq+ 0.974 / 0.872.
limits: Needs a reference formalization, so it cannot judge brand-new maths.
agent_relevance: Use equivalence checking against a trusted reference when one exists; type-check alone misranks methods.

source: Poiroux et al. (2025) Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization
finding: BEq+ is precise but misses many correct formalizations; recall is the weak side, and worse on long statements.
numbers: ProofNetVerif, 3752 pairs, 1142 equivalent. BEqL: precision 100.0, recall 30.9, F1 47.2. BEq+: precision 98.0, recall 48.3, F1 64.7. BEq+ recall 62.5% on short vs 29.6% on long statements.
limits: Original BEq paper reported recall 67.14% on a different 200-sample set; not comparable.
agent_relevance: A positive equivalence signal is trustworthy; a negative one is weak evidence. Use it as a one-sided check.

source: Poiroux et al. (2025) Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization
finding: The public Lean 4 ports of ProofNet had many errors, so earlier reported numbers on them were biased.
numbers: 118 of 371 entries (31.8%) had formalization errors in the two Lean 4 ports; corrected as ProofNet#.
limits: Reference-free metrics (human grade, type-check) are unaffected.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks and reference answers can be wrong; a scaffold should not treat any single reference as ground truth.

source: Poiroux et al. (2025) Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization
finding: Sampling many candidates, filtering by type-check, and picking by similarity raises accuracy without training.
numbers: GPT-4o on ProofNet# validation: 31.0% single generation, 45.1% with 50 samples + type-check filter + selection heuristic. Samples tested up to n=1000.
limits: Gains flatten with n; type-check filter helps most; majority vote without filter barely helps.
agent_relevance: Best-of-n with a hard validity filter and a consistency-based selector is a cheap, tested lift.

source: Poiroux et al. (2025) Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization
finding: Research-level statements are very hard without file context, and fine-tuning on existing data did not help there.
numbers: RLM25: 619 pairs from six Lean blueprint projects. BEq+ for GPT-4o: 12-shot 1.50%, full file context 20.64%, context minus proofs 24.56%, minus theorems and proofs 17.20%. Llemma 34B: 0.79 / 25.99 / 30.33 (12-shot / full / minus proofs). Fine-tuned models (MMA, Lean Workbook) did not beat base models.
limits: Contamination judged unlikely by cutoff dates; statements only, not proofs; BEq+ is a lower bound.
agent_relevance: Context (definitions in scope, nearby lemmas) is the strongest moderator; give the agent the local library, not just the sentence.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Multilingual Mathematical Autoformalization
finding: Training on GPT-4 informalizations of Isabelle and Lean libraries (MMA, 332K pairs) lifted a base LLaMA-33B from 0% to 16-18% acceptable statements.
numbers: Manual check of 100 problems each on miniF2F and ProofNet: base model 0% acceptable with no or minor correction; fine-tuned 16-18%. Compile rates (miniF2F/ProofNet): Isabelle-only model, Isabelle output 36/30; joint model, Isabelle 24/18; Lean4-only model, Lean4 14/6; joint model, Lean4 20/4.
limits: Joint training beat single-language on Lean4 miniF2F compile (20 vs 14) but not on Isabelle compile rate or Lean4 ProofNet (4 vs 6); the paper says quality was better with joint data. Small manual sample; the intro says 50 outputs, methods say 100.
agent_relevance: Cheap synthetic data from the easy direction (informalize) trains the hard direction; compile rate and quality diverge across conditions.

source: Ying et al. (2024) Lean Workbook
finding: Iterative loop with compile check, back-translation plus NLI check, and human repair of failures built a 57K Lean 4 problem set with high sampled accuracy.
numbers: Six rounds; 205,079 outputs compile; 57,231 pass the NLI check; manual check of a random sample: 93.5% accurate. 341 human-corrected problems added to training. 21 new IMO statements formalized.
limits: Manual sample is small (5-10 per tag); the authors note compile-passing outputs often do not follow the question.
agent_relevance: Layered filters (compile, back-translate check, human sample) cut 205K to 57K (28% survive); the filters, not the model, create the quality.

source: Ying et al. (2024) Lean Workbook
finding: The NLI and compile filters are imperfect gates: a higher automatic pass rate did not mean fewer errors.
numbers: Adding Lean Workbook Plus data gave a higher NLI pass rate, but human review found more number theory mistakes.
limits: Qualitative statement in the paper; no counts extracted.
agent_relevance: Automatic semantic checks can drift or be gamed; keep an independent sample audit.

source: Gao et al. (2024) Herald: A Natural Language Annotated Lean 4 Dataset
finding: A Mathlib-derived dataset with hierarchical informalization lifted statement translation much on competition problems and modestly on graduate-level text.
numbers: Herald translator: miniF2F-test 96.7%, valid 96.3%, internal textbook theorems 23.5%, College COT 16.0% (intro; abstract of v2 says 93.2% Pass@128 and 22.5%). Baselines InternLM2-Math-Plus-7B 73.0% / 7.5%; TheoremLlama 55.0% / 4.0%.
limits: Accuracy means passing the Lean compiler and an LLM back-translation check, not human equivalence; abstract and intro numbers differ within one paper; internal dataset not public.
agent_relevance: Near-ceiling contest scores hide a sharp drop on textbook-level statements (96.7% to 23.5%).

source: Gao et al. (2024) Herald: A Natural Language Annotated Lean 4 Dataset
finding: Augmentation ablation: adding tactic-based and informal-based synthetic data raised ProofNet validation accuracy from 50.0% to 68.3%.
numbers: Dataset ratio 1:0:0 gives ProofNet-valid 50.0%, miniF2F-test 86.8%; ratio 1:1:1 gives ProofNet-valid 68.3%, miniF2F-test 91.4%, Extract-Theorem 17.5%.
limits: Metric is the validation pipeline pass with 128 samples, not strict human grading.
agent_relevance: Synthetic augmentation and 128-sample coverage matter; pass@k is generous.

source: Gao et al. (2024) Herald: A Natural Language Annotated Lean 4 Dataset
finding: The authors human-graded outputs on ProofNet validation and found dataset errors there, and say the LLM back-translation check is not perfectly accurate.
numbers: 128 translations per item over 185 ProofNet validation statements; first validated output graded as correct, minor error or major error.
limits: Exact grade counts not extracted from the text read.
agent_relevance: Corroborates the ProofNet error finding from Poiroux and the weakness of LLM-as-judge alignment checks.

source: Lu et al. (2024) Process-Driven Autoformalization in Lean 4
finding: Using Lean compiler feedback during training (process supervision) improved Lean 4 autoformalization with less filtered data; strong LLMs still scored low on the new ForML4 test sets.
numbers: ForML4 covers statements and proofs; GPT-4 greedy compile success on the Real test 10.20%; closed-source models clearly above open-source on greedy and pass@k.
limits: Work-in-progress version; metrics are compile rate and human scores; full table numbers beyond GPT-4 Real not extracted.
agent_relevance: Compiler error messages are a usable intermediate signal for repair loops.

source: Agrawal et al. (2022) Towards a Mathematics Formalisation Assistant using LLMs
finding: Input-dependent prompt selection plus elaboration filtering and voting let Codex formalize undergraduate statements in Lean with about 75% accuracy.
numbers: 120 statements (3 sets of 40: false, silly, theorem). Elaborated / correct / some correct / all wrong: false statements 32/21/28/4; silly 34/26/32/2; theorem 33/30/30/3. Fixed prompts: none of 15 completions elaborated in the worked example.
limits: 15-20 completions at temperature 0.8; counts are among elaborated completions; 11 statements were already in mathlib (23 of 29 still elaborated without them); Lean 3 era.
agent_relevance: Filter by elaboration, then vote by definitional equality: early evidence for the sample, validate, select pattern.

source: Agrawal et al. (2022) Towards a Mathematics Formalisation Assistant using LLMs
finding: Elaboration success is a decent but imperfect proxy for correctness. Wrong answers clustered on concepts with few prompts.
numbers: Theorem statements: 30 of 33 elaborated were correct (91%); false statements 21 of 32 (66%); silly statements 26 of 34 (76%).
limits: Small samples; proofs were a case study only (13 theorems, with at least one of twelve completions repairable).
agent_relevance: Validity depends on input oddness; false or odd inputs yield more plausible-but-wrong formalizations.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Consistent Autoformalization for Constructing Mathematical Libraries
finding: Retrieval of most-similar examples, denoising, and syntax-error feedback improve consistency; retrieval helped small models close the gap to larger ones.
numbers: MS-RAG uses BM25 top-3 exemplars. Mistral 7B with MS-RAG beats Mixtral 8x7B with fixed prompts on all metrics and is comparable to GPT-3.5 without MS-RAG on some metrics. One metric shows +15.83 for a model with MS-RAG.
limits: Isabelle ZF library domain; metrics are similarity metrics (BLEU, RUBY), not human equivalence.
agent_relevance: Retrieval from the target library beats bigger models; matches Azerbayev and Poiroux findings.

source: Ye et al. (2024) FormalAlign: Automated Alignment Evaluation for Autoformalization
finding: A trained alignment scorer beat GPT-4 at spotting misaligned formalizations, showing wrong-but-valid statements are common enough to need their own detector.
numbers: Alignment-Selection Score 99.21% vs GPT-4 88.91% on FormL4-Basic (+11.58 points reported); 66.39% vs 64.34% on MiniF2F-Valid (+3.19 reported).
limits: Negatives are synthetic misalignments; gain on miniF2F is small.
agent_relevance: Example in paper: dropping a unit still compiles and is logically valid. A scaffold needs a fidelity check beyond the compiler.

source: Murphy et al. (2024) Autoformalizing Euclidean Geometry
finding: Diagram-heavy geometry is hard. GPT-4 got 18.9% of theorems right with 5-shot; GPT-4V got 21.0%. Delegating implicit diagram facts to an SMT solver made proofs feasible.
numbers: LeanEuclid: GPT-4 5-shot 18.9% theorems; GPT-4V 21.0%; GPT-4V 23.1% of proofs; SMT-based automatic semantic evaluation.
limits: Euclid's Elements plus UniGeo problems only.
agent_relevance: Split the task: have a symbolic tool fill in implicit structure so the LLM writes only explicit steps.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning
finding: Autoformalization to first-order logic plus a prover helps a lot on synthetic data but does not beat chain-of-thought for GPT-4 on natural data.
numbers: ProofWriter balanced subset: GPT-3.5 96.4%, GPT-4 98.3% with LINC. FOLIO: GPT-4 CoT 75.3% vs LINC 72.5% average, McNemar p=0.58 (not significant). On FOLIO, precision on True/False 93% (LINC) vs 81% (CoT); recall 60% vs 75%.
limits: ProofWriter is synthetic with short sentences; FOLIO is naturalistic. LINC errors are localized to the parsing step.
agent_relevance: A formal back end gives high precision and low recall; translation is the bottleneck on natural language.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning
finding: FOL translation yields syntax errors in smaller models and some in GPT-4; formalization errors cause wrong answers on real data.
numbers: FOL syntax errors: 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4. LINC mispredictions overlap little with CoT (similarity 0.14-0.22 vs 0.52-0.56 among in-context methods).
limits: Only FOLIO and ProofWriter; bootstrapped 10-way majority vote.
agent_relevance: Formal-route and plain-reasoning errors differ, so combining routes helps; keep both.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM
finding: LLM translation to symbolic form plus a solver beats standard and CoT prompts; self-refinement with solver errors raises executable rate but accuracy plateaus.
numbers: GPT-3.5 average gain 39.2% over standard prompting and 18.4% over CoT across five datasets. GPT-4 executable rate 79.9% on FOLIO and 32.6% on AR-LSAT. Self-refinement raised executable rate by 5.01 on average; accuracy stagnates after early rounds while executable rate keeps rising.
limits: Fallback to CoT when the formulation does not run; synthetic sets are near 100% executable; CoT gave -3.2 on AR-LSAT.
agent_relevance: Syntax feedback fixes grammar, not meaning: repeated refine rounds give diminishing accuracy.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models
finding: Declarative formalization handed to a SAT/SMT solver was tested against program-aided reasoning on logic and arithmetic tasks.
numbers: PDF downloaded but numbers not extracted in this pass.
limits: No exact figures recorded; check the paper before citing.
agent_relevance: Declarative specifications may be easier for LLMs to write than step-by-step programs.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove
finding: Translating an informal proof into a formal sketch and letting an automated prover fill the gaps beat prior neural provers on miniF2F.
numbers: With human informal proofs: 42.6% valid, 39.3% test (200 of 488 problems). Codex and Minerva 8B informal proofs both gave 40.6% valid and 35.3% test. Baselines on test: Thor 29.9%, Thor + expert iteration 35.2%.
limits: Draft quality matters; ablations in the paper shrink the gain.
agent_relevance: Sketch-level formalization with a prover filling details tolerates imperfect translation.

source: Zheng et al. (2022) miniF2F
finding: miniF2F fixed 488 contest statements across proof systems, creating the first shared yardstick for statement translation and proving.
numbers: 488 problems; formalized for several systems. Wu et al. note Isabelle formalizations were committed in March 2022.
limits: Narrow scope (high-school algebra and number theory); near ceiling by 2024-25 (Herald 96.7%).
agent_relevance: Contest-level scores overstate ability; use harder, library-grounded sets.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) Autoformalization in the Era of Large Language Models: A Survey
finding: Survey of workflow from data to evaluation, with emphasis on semantic consistency, hallucination, and use of autoformalization to verify LLM outputs.
numbers: Lists open-source models and datasets (DeepSeek-Prover, Herald, Lean Workbook, Kimina, Goedel); cites a Qwen2.5-72B formal reasoning model at 80.7% on miniF2F.
limits: Secondary source; numbers are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Supports the framing that autoformalization can be a verifier for LLM outputs, not just for math.

source: Yu et al. (2025) FormalMATH
finding: A human-in-the-loop pipeline with multi-LLM autoformalization, semantic verification and negation-based disproof filtering kept 72.09% of statements before manual check.
numbers: 5,560 verified statements; 30.1% of candidates survive to LLM verification and 21.7% end in the benchmark. 12 Olympiad-medalist annotators, 22 days, 6.89 USD per statement. Disproof filter removed 1.6%. Best prover 16.46%.
limits: Most candidates still fail; semantic verification is LLM then human expert, not formal equivalence.
agent_relevance: Trying to prove the negation catches false formalizations cheaply.
